task_master_1.title: Potentiality
task_master_1.tagline: Potentiality is Facinating but Actuality is Power.
task_master_1.description: Aristotle’s concept of an “unmoved mover” is grounded in the difference between potentiality and actuality. According to his definitions, potentials cannot self-actualize. Coins do not flip themselves, nor do they flip for absolutely no reason whatsoever. Seeds have to fall into fertile soil in order to grow. Airplanes do not spontaneously fly, nor do they simply go from stationary to flying by their own actions. In other words, potentiality can only become actuality when potential is made actual by some outside force. That force’s influence, in turn, was also a potential made actual, and so on. This implies a chain of actions: each change is a potential made actual by some separate, prior set of circumstances. This chain cannot continue forever, however. Without an uncaused cause, there would never have been any “actuality” at all. There must be one thing that is pure actuality, with no potentiality: an unmoved mover. While Aristotle did not identify this original actuality with the Judeo-Christian God, specifically, the concepts are notably similar.
task_master_1.fiction_novel_section_description: The Unmoved Mover is a central concept in Aristotle's philosophy, representing the ultimate source of all motion and change in the universe. According to Aristotle, the Unmoved Mover is a purely actual being, devoid of potentiality, and the cause of all actuality in the cosmos. The Unmoved Mover is the prime mover, the first cause, and the ultimate explanation for the existence and order of the world. By contemplating the nature of the Unmoved Mover, readers can gain insights into the fundamental principles governing reality and the relationship between potentiality and actuality.
task_master_1.fiction_novel_section_tagline: The Unmoved Mover is a central concept in Aristotle's philosophy, representing the ultimate source of all motion and change in the universe.

task_master_2.title: Direction
task_master_2.tagline: It is direction itself that hinders us from finding our way.
task_master_2.description: The concept of direction is a fundamental aspect of human experience. It guides our actions, shapes our decisions, and influences our perceptions of the world. Direction is both a physical and metaphorical concept, representing the path we choose to follow in life. It is the compass that guides us through the complexities of existence, helping us navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and fulfill our potential. By understanding the power of direction and aligning our actions with our values and goals, we can create a purposeful and fulfilling life that reflects our truest aspirations. Part of the teaching of Dante is that deliverance comes from rising above the cycles and circles of a worldly life. The cycles are connected with the spiritless, sinful lives of the people in the town, whereas Petrarch and Dante intend to live their lives towards enlightenment and Christian Heaven, aiming for higher places with every action. So rather than choose a direct path that would have him follow the lead of one who has attained enlightenment, such as Augustine, Petrarch chooses a path that might be described as moving along ground level, seeking through the natural paths and waters, through the streets of the town, to achieve his own progression. In this way, the novel is full of contradicting directions of flow and influence. The path upward is elusive and the path along is repetitive and cyclical. Perhaps it is direction itself that is hindering Petrarch from finding his way? When he allows himself to live by the river, without following or seeking a particular path, his lack of direction makes sense, and mimics the river itself. The river seems to be flowing one way, another, falling over a cliff as a waterfall, halted and meandering, unchanged by time, never beginning or ending. It is the vision of this wholeness that brings light to Petrarch thinking and purpose to his life’s wandering. Enlightenment had been associated with height and a journey upwards, but Petrarch’s searching shows that enlightenment is not ascending above the rest of the world but rather recognizing one’s equality with it. And, fittingly, the novel ends with Petrarch face to face with his childhood friend, not above but together with the world.
task_master_2.fiction_novel_section_description: The Magus of Power is a novel that explores the themes of direction, purpose, and enlightenment through the journey of the protagonist, Petrarch. As he navigates the challenges and complexities of life, Petrarch grapples with questions of identity, meaning, and destiny, seeking to find his true path and fulfill his potential. The novel delves into the power of direction in shaping our lives, guiding our choices, and influencing our relationships with others. Through Petrarch's quest for enlightenment and self-discovery, readers are invited to reflect on their own journey and the direction they choose to follow in life.
task_master_2.fiction_novel_section_tagline: The Magus of Power is a novel that explores the themes of direction, purpose, and enlightenment through the journey of the protagonist, Petrarch.
